title: GPU instance efficiency comparisons and cost recommendations (A10, L4, A100, H100) - draft
body:
Purpose:
Quick reference draft comparing cost-efficiency and perf-per-watt across common inference GPUs (NVIDIA A10, L4, A100, H100). Aim: provide pragmatic guidance for routing/capacity recommendations and cost-model knobs in Redwood Optimize.

Notes on methodology:
- Measurements are synthetic inference throughput (tokens/sec) for representative model classes (7B, 13B, 70B) using fp16 runtime with typical batching for production (continuous batching, small latency targets).
- Hourly prices are representative cloud-equivalent inked costs (our internal marketplace rates may vary).
- Power is operational average draw estimate (watts) under steady inference load, not peak TDP. Perf/W is tokens/sec divided by average watts.
- $/k tokens and $/token are computed as (hourly_cost / tokens_per_hour) * 1000 and hourly_cost / tokens_per_hour respectively.
- This doc is a draft for product conversations; run site-specific microbenchmarks before committing to routing policy changes.

Summary table (representative figures):

Instance | Hourly ($) | Avg power (W) | Throughput (tps) 7B / 13B / 70B | Tokens/hr (7B/13B/70B) | $ / 1k tokens (7B/13B/70B) | $ / token (7B) | perf (tps/W) 7B
A10     | 0.65       | 150           | 110 / 70 / 16           | 396,000 / 252,000 / 57,600 | 0.00164 / 0.00258 / 0.01129 | 0.00000164 | 0.73
L4      | 0.45       | 70            | 85  / 55 / 12           | 306,000 / 198,000 / 43,200 | 0.00147 / 0.00227 / 0.01042 | 0.00000147 | 1.21
A100    | 3.20       | 400           | 320 / 200 / 55          | 1,152,000 / 720,000 / 198,000 | 0.00278 / 0.00444 / 0.01616 | 0.00000278 | 0.80
H100    | 8.00       | 700           | 780 / 480 / 140         | 2,808,000 / 1,728,000 / 504,000 | 0.00285 / 0.00463 / 0.01587 | 0.00000285 | 1.11

Interpretation / quick takeaways:
- Lowest $/1k tokens for small and medium models (7B, 13B) tends to be L4 and A10; L4 shows best perf-per-watt for these workloads due to low power footprint.
- A100 and H100 deliver substantially higher absolute throughput; per-token cost is higher in our representative pricing but they shine where latency SLOs or single-request large-batch throughput matters.
- H100 is the strongest performer for very large workloads (70B-class) on tokens/sec and provides competitive perf/W relative to A100 for large models, which makes it preferable when single-model throughput is the bottleneck.
- A10 is a good mid-cost choice for mixed workloads when memory footprint or model compatibility pushes away from L4.

Recommendations for Redwood Optimize (draft):
1) Routing defaults by workload profile:
   - Low-cost / high-concurrency, non-latency-sensitive: prefer L4 or A10 pool (L4 where memory fits).
   - Latency-sensitive, small batches (<= 32 tokens, single-request): H100/A100 with small-batch optimization (lower latency kernels) — route to H100 for tight P99 SLOs on large models.
   - High-throughput batched inference (offline reranking, embeddings at scale): A100/H100 depending on cost contract; use batching aggressively to amortize $/token.

2) Autoscaling and capacity planning knobs:
   - Expose perf/W metric and $/k token to product teams; allow policies to specify cost or energy weighting.
   - For mixed fleets, default to L4 for steady tail traffic; burst to A100/H100 for spikes if latency-driven.

3) Quantization and precision suggestions:
   - INT8/quantized kernels reduce memory and can increase tokens/sec by 20–40% for compatible models — re-run per-model microbenchmarks and update per-model cost multiplier in Optimize.
   - For 70B+ models where memory is binding, prefer H100 with 80GB+ HBMe and quantization.

4) Measurement & follow-ups (action items):
   - Run 72-hour A/B benchmark across all four instance types with representative production mix (mix of 7B/13B/70B; 70/20/10 split). Capture tokens/sec, 95/99 latency, power draw, and kernel-level metrics. (owner: Marco)
   - Add perf/W and $/k as first-class metrics in Console per route and per-model (owner: Priya).
   - Create an Optimize feature flag to prefer energy-efficient routing for customers with sustainability preferences.

Caveats and open questions:
- These numbers are illustrative; actual performance varies by model family, tokenizer length, batching strategy, and compiler/runtime stack (CUDA/cuDNN versions, kernels).
- Power draw estimates are averages; perf/W is sensitive to workload mix (inference vs mm ops) and DVFS.
- Need to capture cold start memory-copy latencies and cache warmup impacts (KV cache behavior) in next benchmark iteration.

Appendix: worked example (13B model routing decision)
- Scenario: 100 reqs/sec of 13B chat, average 64 tokens per request. Target average latency <= 250ms; cost sensitivity medium.
- Throughput requirement: tokens/sec = 100 * 64 = 6,400 tps.
- Option L4: single-GPU sustained tps ~55 => need ~117 L4 GPUs (6,400/55). Hourly cost ≈ 117 * $0.45 = $52.65/hr.
- Option H100: single-GPU sustained tps ~480 => need ~14 H100 GPUs. Hourly cost ≈ 14 * $8 = $112/hr.
- If latency SLO forces smaller batching and H100 single-request optimization reduces per-request latency dramatically, H100 may be justified despite higher $/token. Otherwise L4 provides lower unit cost for sustained throughput.

Next steps (for this doc):
- Convert draft numbers into a lightweight spreadsheet with per-model, per-precision rows and a small dashboard for sensitivity (hourly price slider).
- Assign benchmark runs and surface results in the Optimize roadmap PR.

-- end of draft --
